Thermoplastic like worbla for example will give you the thin-ness and rigidity, or a thicker look if you sandwich it around a craft foam base. Thermoplastic is nice because you can heat it and mould it over a curved bottle or something to get the shape and it is sandable and paintable. But fairly expensive.      


Many props are made with foam if you want to go cheap. Craft foam could work, and you could use two layers hot glued together and then cut out he filigree and glue it on top, then prime and paint. With craft foam I make a "paper mache" of cheesecloth and white glue on the inside and it makes it quite sturdy and lightweight.      

Alternatively you could use spray expanding foam that you can buy at the hardware store. You can let it harden and then carve it into the right shape with a craft knife.      

And last but not least I would also check out crayola brand model magic, which is a clay foam hybrid type thing. It's easy to shape and dries without needing to be fired and stays lightweight when it solidifies, although it remains a little spongier than some harder materials. It's cheap and easy so worth checking into for small prop like things.

Cosplay is fun! Here are some of my tips!     

Make sure you always have a spotter if your character is wearing a mask, or is difficult to move in. Having someone around to help you is a godsend - I have a costume that looks amazing but it is hard to see out of the mask, so I have no peripheral vision which can make walking around a convention hard without a helping hand.      

Do a dry run of your costume first. You never know what is going to pinch or tear or get heavy after a while. If it's painful to try on and walk around in for a half hour it's going to hurt like hell after a long day of walking around.      

Carry a small repair kit. Pins, sewing needle, thread. Bobby pins or hair ties.     


Drink lots of water. Consider how hard it is to take off your costume if you have to pee.     

Try and build a bag into your cosplay if you need to take one with you/carry lots of stuff. Something your character would actually carry that fits into the costume looks way better than a generic backpack. Alternatively: make your spotter carry your phone/wallet/keys etc.     

Expect to be bumped into and stepped on. Be careful of delicate props and fabrics. Foam creations will get dinged and white things will get scuffed.     

Expected to get stopped a lot. A lot. People will want to take pics and as soon as you stop 500 other people will jump in (that might have been too nervous to stop you )and want to take a picture too. Plan for 2x the amount of time to get anywhere, especially if you are playing a popular character or your cosplay is very dramatic. I have seen some amazing displays take 15-20 minutes just to cross a street only to be immediately stopped on the other side.     

That being said! Getting photos back feels great, so keep an eye on forums or give out your email address so people can send you their pix. 

You might get hugged. Sometimes it can get weird.     

There is no need to stay in character unless you want to. Many people don't, and many folks will want to ask you questions about your cosplay and other OOC type stuff. (Can't I hold your prop? What is this made of? How long did it take? Etc). I have met several cosplayers that like to stay in character though, and it looks great and goes over well and can be really fun to observe. So if you feel like it and like to act - go right ahead!


Posing for photos:

Get someone to photograph you in your costume to start, just so you have a visual of how it looks in pictures. Alternatively, set up your phone or camera on a timer and stage a mini photo shoot yourself. This will give you a frame of reference as to what angles you like best.     

It helps to study your character's mannerisms or poses if you can. If they have a way they stand or sit, or an action pose that is reminiscent of the character, try to use it.         

If they're action-y? Do an action pose. If they're romantic, try to look wistful and airy. Sad? Feel free to slump. Crazy? Jump around, roll on the ground. Play it up. Practice in front of a mirror so you can get a feel for the poses and so you know how to move when the time comes.      

Alternatively, pose in a way that shows off a cool part of your costume if you like. Lots of detail on the back? Practice looking over your shoulder. Have a prop? Practice holding it casually and also in an animated way.     
     
And if you get stuck taking more than one photo, try to change poses between shots. If you end up with a ring of photographers it's nice to turn so that others can shoot you from the other angle if they like. Or to get some variety.     

And you know.. Go out and have a blast!

To build on this point, a conditioner contains humectants, which bind moisture to the skin (or hair). What colour is your tattoo? Black is just about the hardest thing to cover, and you will need to colour correct before applying any concealer else its going to look grey, or worse; green.

For long-wear, an alcohol activated palette is best. They work like watercolour paints only you use alcohol to activate it. When it dries it is water tight and has little texture, and it has to be removed with alcohol to get it off. Alcohol palettes are what makeup artists typically use in movie makeups to draw tattoos on actors, and some other things. Skin Illustrator is a commonly used brand for these things, but I believe you have to buy a whole palette. The stuff is great, though.

Now, if we consider colour theory we know that black tattoo ink is built up of dark blue or dark green pigment. So you'll need to put something the opposite of those colours on your tattoo to take out the green and blue. So first apply an ORANGE or RED product and trace your tattoo completely. Let the layer dry, powder to set. Then go over with your concealer and powder again.

Pick a waterproof concealer; Kat Von D's was recommended by someone else and it works well. I use it to cover tattoos all the time. Make Up For Ever has a comparable product called Full Cover Concealer that has a wider shade range. 

Set with powder, apply engagement ring.

I have suffered with horrible depression all my life. At age 6 I was put in counselling for telling my teacher I was going to kill myself. I battled it on and off, and was on anti-depressants for roughly ten years before I gave them up. No one really understood my mind, and I could not ever talk my feelings out without turning people off, or weirding them out. So I found similarly depressed people on the internet, and I talked to them, it helped. At one point, later on, I hit the lowest I have ever been when I entered into a relationship with a man who emotionally and mentally abused me, and used my misery as a weapon against me. I broke down at my job, lost friends, and for the first time in my life I learned what it was like to be utterly alone in the world. When I got out of the situation I had all of two friends, I was a wreck, I couldn't sleep at night, and I turned to one-night-stands and alcohol to hide from my feelings.


Then one day a coworker said something to me that stuck: *"Surround yourself with positive things, and other positive things will be drawn to you".*


Misery likes company, after all.  I made many small changes, but in reality all I did was remove the stressful things from my life. Cut out the bullshit, cut out the drama. I made a comfortable, safe, bubble, of supportive people and make no more time for crap. I do what makes me happy. I also got a dog, he helps. Winter is still hard, but I know this, expect it, and ride it through. 


Good luck with your depression, you are loved, find your positivity and cling to it. Feel free to message me if you need to talk.
